78.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
78.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
78.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing devotional songs, and at the hour of Krishna's birth ring bells and rock a small cradle holding an image of baby Krishna; in Maharashtra the next day, teams form human pyramids to break a pot of curds hung high, as Krishna the butter thief would.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the driver. Krishna chose to hold the reins for Arjuna, and the stories camp closed. Today, the driver's first night.

A prison cell in the city of Mathura. Midnight, a storm outside. A mother, Devaki, and a father, Vasudeva, in chains. Her brother, the tyrant king Kamsa, was told at her wedding that her eighth child would kill him. So he locked them up and took every baby they had. Now the eighth is coming. Last time, Krishna was a grown man holding a chariot's reins; tonight's festival goes back to the very start. And the whole night is one question: can a newborn be carried out of a locked prison, across a flooding river, before morning?
screen: `A PRISON AT MIDNIGHT.` → `KAMSA FEARS THE EIGHTH CHILD.` → `CAN A BABY GET OUT BY MORNING?`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it like this. At midnight, the baby is born. The guards fall into a deep sleep. The chains fall from Vasudeva's wrists. The prison doors swing open on their own. Vasudeva puts his newborn son in a basket on his head and walks out into the storm, to the river Yamuna, in flood. And the river, in the story, lets him through; in a popular telling, the water rises to touch the baby's feet, then parts. The great serpent Shesha rises behind him and spreads his many hoods over the basket like an umbrella against the rain. On the far side, in the village of Gokul, the cowherd's wife Yashoda has just given birth to a daughter. Vasudeva quietly swaps the babies and walks back to his cell. The doors close. The chains return. In the morning Kamsa comes for the child, and the baby girl slips from his hands, rises into the sky as a goddess, and tells him: the one you fear is already born, somewhere else. So Krishna grows up hidden among cowherds, a mischievous boy stealing butter. That's Janmashtami: janma, birth, and ashtami, the eighth day of the moon's dark half, when tradition says he was born. Households that keep the festival fast all day and stay up until midnight, singing, and at the hour of the birth they ring bells and rock a tiny cradle. In the Gita, Krishna says he comes, age after age, whenever goodness declines. Janmashtami celebrates that promise: the good doesn't always arrive at noon. Sometimes it comes at midnight, in the dark, carried through a storm.
screen: `THE CHAINS FALL, THE DOORS OPEN.` · `THE RIVER PARTS; THE SERPENT SHELTERS.` · `A BABY SWAPPED IN GOKUL.` · `JANMA + ASHTAMI: BIRTH ON THE EIGHTH.`

segments.voice: Dim the lights or close your eyes, and sit in the dark with something good you're still waiting for: healing, a reconciliation, a job, a change in someone you love. Let the waiting be here, the way the family waited in the cell. Then picture a single small light, the door opening just a crack, without forcing it.
Janmashtami. Janma, birth; ashtami, the eighth day. The midnight birthday of Krishna.
Your line: the good arrives at midnight. Even in a locked room, in a storm. Happy Janmashtami.

79.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
79.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
79.carry: welcome it, then let it go
79.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
79.howItsDone: For Ganesh Chaturthi, Hindu families and neighborhoods install clay images of Ganesha at home or in public pandals, worship him with lamps, flowers, durva grass and modaks for one and a half to ten days, then immerse the image in water in a joyful procession; many now choose unpainted clay or eco-friendly images.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, a baby carried out of a prison through a flood at midnight. The good arrives at midnight.

Drums so loud you feel them in your chest, in the streets of a city in Maharashtra at the end of summer. Families walk home carrying a Ganesha made of clay, some small enough to hold in two hands, some so huge they ride on trucks, trunk and belly and all. Children shout a name. You met this god at the start of the stories camp: the boy at the door, the elephant head, the broken tusk, the mouse, the sweets. Today is the festival where he comes to stay, for a few days. Then, on purpose, everyone lets him go.
screen: `DRUMS IN THE STREETS.` → `A CLAY GANESHA CARRIED HOME.` → `HE STAYS, THEN GOES.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth: the fourth day of the moon's bright half, in the late-summer month of Bhadrapada, the day tradition celebrates as Ganesha's birthday. In many homes it goes like this. The clay image comes in, and a priest or a family elder invites Ganesha to be present in it, as a guest. For the next days he's the most honored visitor you've ever had: lamps morning and evening, flowers, blades of durva grass, which he loves, and modaks, the sweet dumplings, the same sweets you met as prasad, the offering that comes back. Friends come to visit him. Then, after a day and a half, or three, five, seven or ten days, depending on the family, comes the hardest part. The family carries him to the sea, a river, a lake or a tank of water, with drums and dancing, and gently gives him back. The clay melts. The crowds call out Ganpati Bappa Morya, and then a second line in Marathi that means: come back soon next year. For centuries it was mostly a home festival. In 1893, in Pune, the leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public celebration, and the huge street festivals grew from there. Why melt him? Many teachers explain it this way: the clay comes from the earth and returns to it. The form is there so people can welcome something they can't see, and letting it go says the god was never trapped in the clay. It's also a rehearsal: everything you love, you welcome and one day let go. The festival makes that joyful.
screen: `CHATURTHI: THE FOURTH DAY.` · `AN HONORED GUEST, WITH MODAKS.` · `GIVEN BACK TO THE WATER.` · `WELCOMED, THEN LET GO, WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Hold something small in your hands, a cup, a stone, a ring, and welcome it the way a family welcomes Ganesha: really look at it, really be glad it's here. Then slowly set it down in front of you and open your hands. Notice what it feels like to let go of something you love, gently, without dropping it.
Ganesh Chaturthi. The fourth day, when Ganesha is welcomed home in clay, honored for days, and given back to the water.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. The clay goes back to the earth. Seventy-nine days, and counting.

80.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
80.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
80.howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess over nine nights in regional ways: garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, displays of dolls (golu) in the south, fasting and recitation of the Devi Mahatmya in many homes; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates the victory of good.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, a clay god welcomed home and given back to the water. Welcome it, then let it go.

Eleven at night in Gujarat, and an open ground is packed. People in mirrored skirts and embroidered jackets move in huge circles, clapping, spinning, sticks clicking in rhythm. They'll be back tomorrow night, and the night after: nine nights in a row. Far to the east, in Bengal, neighborhoods build glittering temporary halls for a ten-armed goddess on a lion. In the south, families set out steps of dolls. Different places, different customs, the same nine nights. And at the center of many of them, one story: a demon nobody could defeat, and the Goddess who did.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS OF DANCING.` → `A TEN-ARMED GODDESS ON A LION.` → `A DEMON NOBODY COULD DEFEAT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text recited in homes and temples during these nights. Mahishasura, a demon who is part buffalo, grows so powerful that he drives the gods out of heaven. In a popular telling, he'd won a boon that no man or god could kill him. The gods are so furious that their anger bursts out of them as light, and the light of every god flows together into one blazing form: a woman. The Goddess. Each god hands her a weapon: Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, and a lion to ride. People call her Durga, the one who is hard to reach, hard to defeat. She rides out laughing, and the battle begins. Mahishasura keeps changing shape to escape her: a buffalo, a lion, a warrior with a sword, an elephant, a buffalo again. She meets every form. Finally, as he struggles half out of the buffalo's body, she puts her foot on his neck and ends it. That's why images of Durga so often show her spear in a buffalo. Navaratri means nine nights: nava, nine, and ratri, night. Some honor nine forms of the Goddess, one each night. Some fast. Some dance the garba in her honor. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, the tenth of victory, is when the good wins. In much of north India it's also Dussehra, when Rama's victory over Ravana is celebrated with huge effigies of the ten-headed king going up in flames. Different regions tell the victory through different stories, and the festival brings each of them to the same tenth morning.
screen: `THE GODS' LIGHT BECOMES THE GODDESS.` · `DURGA MEETS EVERY FORM HE TAKES.` · `NAVA + RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · `THE TENTH DAY: THE GOOD WINS.`

segments.voice: Sit up tall, like someone riding a lion, and think of one small, ordinary thing that keeps changing shape on you: the urge to snap at someone, the scroll that eats your evening, the voice that says you're not enough. Notice how it shifts forms to get past you. Then calmly name it, and decide: not tonight, just for tonight.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and on the tenth day, victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. The good gets the tenth day. See you tomorrow.

81.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
81.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
81.howItsDone: For Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli patterns at the door, light rows of clay lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, and visit relatives; customs and the stories told vary by region over the festival's five days.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day when the good wins. Nine nights, then the dawn.

You already know the night this festival remembers: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana flying home after fourteen years, Bharata waiting with the sandals, and the people of Ayodhya lighting lamps on every wall so he could find his way. Now it's here, for real. The darkest night of the autumn month. The house has been cleaned for days. Someone's drawing a pattern in colored powder on the doorstep. There are sweets in boxes on every surface. And as the sun goes down, a whole country, and families all over the world, start lighting little clay lamps, one after another after another.
screen: `THE NIGHT YOU ALREADY KNOW.` → `COLORED POWDER ON THE DOORSTEP.` → `ONE LAMP, THEN ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: In many places, Diwali is five days, not one. It often starts with a day for buying something new, often a little metal, for good fortune. Then a day that remembers a victory over a demon of darkness. Then the main night, on the new moon, when many families worship Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and well-being, and leave their lights and doors open so she'll come in. Then a day for Krishna lifting a mountain to shelter his village, sometimes marked with a mountain of food. And the fifth day is for brothers and sisters. Not everyone lights the lamps for the same story. In much of the north, it's Rama coming home. In much of the south, it's Krishna defeating a demon king called Narakasura, and people wake before dawn to bathe and celebrate. For many business families, it's Lakshmi, and the start of a new account year. Neighbors share the season too: Jains remember the day Mahavira attained liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the return of Guru Hargobind from prison. Different stories, the same lamps. Why lamps on the darkest night? An old line from the Upanishads, still chanted today, asks to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to what doesn't die. Diwali puts that on a windowsill. You don't argue with the dark. You light a small flame in it, and then another, until someone coming home can see the way.
screen: `FIVE DAYS, NOT ONE.` · `LAKSHMI ON THE DARKEST NIGHT.` · `DIFFERENT STORIES, THE SAME LAMPS.` · `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Light one light if you can: a candle, a small lamp, even a phone screen turned toward you. Think of someone far from home right now, a child away or a friend in another country, or someone lost or lonely who has drifted from the people who love them. Picture your light in a window they could see; you're not pulling them home, just showing the way.
Diwali. The row of lamps, five days, many stories, lit on the darkest night of the month.
Your line: light the way home. One small flame, then another. Day eighty-one, done.

82.title: Holi: the festival of colors
82.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
82.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
82.howItsDone: Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire on the full-moon night of Phalguna and, the next morning, throw colored powder and water with family, neighbors and strangers alike; many use the day to make up after quarrels.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, a whole city lighting lamps for Rama's return. Light the way home.

A street in north India, on a spring morning. Somebody's uncle is purple. A grandmother is laughing with green powder in her hair. A stranger you've never met walks up, says happy Holi, and smears pink on your cheek, and you do the same back. Water balloons from a balcony. Drums from somewhere. By noon you can't tell the banker from the delivery driver, or the neighbor you haven't spoken to in a year from your own cousin. Everyone is the same muddy, glorious color. But the night before, there was a fire, and the fire is where the story is.
screen: `A STRANGER SMEARS PINK ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `NOBODY CAN TELL WHO IS WHO.` → `BUT FIRST, A FIRE.`

segments.voice: The story is about a boy named Prahlad. His father, Hiranyakashipu, is a demon king with a boon that makes him nearly impossible to kill, and he decides that makes him God. Everyone in the kingdom must worship him. His own son won't. Prahlad keeps saying the name of Vishnu. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the father tries everything to stop him: snakes, elephants, a cliff, poison. The boy survives each one. Then comes the part the festival remembers. The king's sister, Holika, is said to be protected from fire. She takes Prahlad on her lap and sits down in a blazing pyre. And the fire turns. Holika burns. The boy walks out unharmed, still saying the name. An honest note: the Bhagavata tells Prahlad's story at length and ends it with Vishnu appearing as Narasimha, half man and half lion. The Holika scene comes from later tellings and from the festival itself, which is how most people know it. So on the full-moon night of Phalguna, at the end of winter, people light bonfires called Holika Dahan, and many walk around them, remembering a fire that couldn't hold a child. The next morning, the colors. People say it with a grin: bura na mano, Holi hai. Don't be offended, it's Holi. For one day the lines between people get smudged on purpose, and old quarrels are supposed to end. Holi has other stories too, and i'll come back for them. But this one starts with the bonfire.
screen: `A BOY WHO KEEPS SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA SITS IN THE FIRE.` · `THE BONFIRE THE NIGHT BEFORE.` · `DON'T BE OFFENDED, IT'S HOLI.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who annoyed you lately, a small hurt, not a deep wound: a curt message, a friend who forgot. Picture that grudge as a dry stick laid on the bonfire the night before Holi, and watch it burn down to ash. Then picture the morning, and that person standing there with color on their face, the same as yours. You don't have to call them; just notice what feels lighter.
Holi. The spring festival of colors, the morning after the bonfire that remembers Prahlad walking out of the fire.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. For one morning, nobody is a stranger. That's day eighty-two.

83.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
83.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
83.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
83.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water, milk or honey over the Shiva lingam with bilva leaves, and keep a vigil through the night chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a fire the night before and colors in the morning. Everyone's the same color today.

This festival happens in the dark. Once a year, on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, just before the new moon, in late winter, Shiva temples stay open all night. The lines go around the block. People carry small brass pots of water and milk. They've been fasting since morning, and they're not going to bed. Inside, the sound doesn't stop: a bell, a chant, Om Namah Shivaya, again and again, until the sky starts to go gray. It's called Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. And one story people tell about it is about a man who stayed awake by accident.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE DARK.` → `TEMPLES OPEN ALL NIGHT.` → `A MAN AWAKE BY ACCIDENT.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Shiva Purana. A hunter goes into the forest, catches nothing all day, and night falls. Afraid of wild animals, he climbs a tree to wait for morning. It happens to be a bilva tree, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And at its foot, hidden in the dark, is a Shiva lingam, the smooth rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples. The hunter has no idea. All night, to stay awake and keep watch, he fidgets, and leaves drop from the branches onto the stone below. Water spills from his flask onto it. He hasn't eaten. He doesn't sleep. By dawn, without meaning to, he has done everything this night asks: fasted, kept awake, offered water and bilva leaves to Shiva. In the tellings, when deer come by he lets them go, and his heart changes. And Shiva frees him. His intention wasn't holy. He was just scared and stuck in a tree. But he stayed. So that's what people do on Shivaratri; ratri means night. They fast, keep a vigil through the night's four watches, and pour water, milk or honey over the lingam, an offering called abhisheka, then lay bilva leaves on top. Different families remember different reasons for the night. Some say it's Shiva's wedding to Parvati. Some say it's when he danced. i'll come back to those. But the practice is the same: don't sleep through it.
screen: `A HUNTER UP A TREE.` · `LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN STONE.` · `HE STAYED, AND THAT WAS ENOUGH.` · `FAST, KEEP WATCH, POUR WATER.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit, close or lower your eyes, and just watch your breath. At some point something in you will say, okay, that's enough, I'm done; don't argue with it, just take three more breaths. Like the hunter on his branch: not holy, just staying.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva. Once a year, the great one, kept awake until dawn.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. The hunter didn't mean to, and staying was enough. Eighty-three days in.

84.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
84.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
84.carry: a thread can hold a promise
84.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists with a lamp, a forehead mark and sweets, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; many families now tie it between sisters, cousins and close friends too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, a hunter up a tree, awake all night. Stay awake for what matters. Today, the smallest festival object there is: a thread.

A summer morning, the full moon of the month of Shravana. In homes across India and far beyond, a sister sets out a small plate: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few sweets, and a thread. Sometimes it's a plain red and gold string. Sometimes it's a glittering thing with a plastic cartoon on it, because her brother is six. She marks his forehead, circles the lamp in front of his face, ties the thread around his wrist, and pops a sweet in his mouth. He gives her a gift, and a promise: I'll look after you. Brothers on other continents get their threads in the mail.
screen: `A PLATE, A LAMP, A THREAD.` → `TIED AROUND HIS WRIST.` → `I'LL LOOK AFTER YOU.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a bond. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is called a rakhi. What's surprising is how small it is. It isn't a contract. You could snap it with two fingers. Yet people keep these threads on for days, sometimes until they fray off, because of what it holds. The best-known story behind it isn't really in the old texts, and it's worth saying so. People tell that Krishna once cut his finger, and Draupadi, without a second thought, tore a strip from the edge of her sari and tied it around the wound. Krishna was moved, and promised to protect her. Years later, in the Mahabharata, Draupadi is dragged into a hall full of men and humiliated, and her sari is pulled. And the cloth doesn't end. It keeps coming, and she's covered. The Mahabharata tells the endless cloth; the torn strip and the promise are how many families tell why. A strip of cloth for a strip of cloth. Notice which way it runs. The one who ties the thread isn't asking for charity. She's offering care first, and the promise answers it. In many families today the thread goes both ways: sisters tie it on sisters, cousins, close friends. And that's the week: a birth at midnight, a clay god welcomed home, nine nights of the Goddess, a row of lamps, a fire and then colors, a night awake, and now a thread.
screen: `RAKSHA — PROTECTION. BANDHAN — A TIE.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO SNAP.` · `A STRIP OF CLOTH FOR A STRIP OF CLOTH.` · `CARE FIRST, THEN THE PROMISE.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Let a face come: a sibling, a child, a parent getting older, a friend having a rough year. Picture tying a thread around their wrist, slowly, the way it's done. Then say it inside, in your own words: I've got you.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection. Small enough to snap, strong enough to hold a promise.
Your line: a thread can hold a promise. The thread is small; the promise isn't. Back tomorrow.
